title: The idols and the axe
hookLine: Ibrahim breaks his people's idols and leaves the biggest one standing with the axe (21:57–58)

lines: THAT'S HOW WE'VE ALWAYS DONE IT.
A KID WHO KEEPS ASKING WHY.
cards: A row of carved figures in a temple, and a young man staring at them. Ibrahim asks his people why they worship them, and gets an answer you may have heard at home: that's how we've always done it.
The Thanksgiving dish nobody actually likes. The route to Grandma's that takes twenty minutes longer. The way we just don't talk about Uncle Ray.
It takes a certain kind of person to keep asking why after that. Usually a kid. And this time, Ibrahim doesn't stop at asking.

teach.b: Surah twenty-one. Ibrahim says to his father and his people, in Pickthall's words: “What are these images unto which ye pay devotion?”

teach.h: WE FOUND OUR FATHERS DOING IT.
teach.b: Their answer, paraphrasing: we found our fathers worshipping them. That's the whole reason. Ibrahim says: then you and your fathers have been plainly wrong.
And he makes a promise: by God, I'll deal with your idols once you've turned your backs and gone. The commentators say the whole town went out to a festival.
While the temple stood empty, he broke the idols into pieces, in Pickthall's words, “all save the chief of them.”
He left the biggest one standing, the verse says, so that they might turn to it. And the axe? The Qur'an never mentions one.
It comes from the commentators' retelling, which says Ibrahim hung the axe on the big idol, or put it in its hand, as if to say: ask him. A vivid detail, and it's tradition, not the verse.
What the verse does give is the trap: a room of smashed statues, and one big one left untouched. When the town comes back, they'll have to decide what they believe that big one can do.

teach.h: ALL SAVE THE CHIEF OF THEM.
teach.b: Ibrahim hasn't made a speech. He's made a question they can't avoid. Sometimes the kindest way to break a habit isn't to argue about it.
It's to let the habit answer for itself.

how: Muslims tell the story of Ibrahim and the idols to children as a lesson in thinking for oneself and in tawhid, and it's read in surahs twenty-one and thirty-seven.

o: Isaac, the son born to Abraham and Sarah
Abraham, the prophet who broke his people's idols
Ishmael, the elder of Abraham's two sons

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: from the commentators, not the verse

s: the Qur'an says Ibrahim left the axe with the biggest idol
the verse never mentions an axe. that detail comes from the commentators' retelling.
his people's reason for the idols was that their fathers worshipped them
we found our fathers worshipping them: that was the whole answer.
Ibrahim broke every idol in the temple
all save the chief of them: he left the biggest standing.

games.q: the town is out at a festival and the temple is empty. you've broken the idols. what do you do with the biggest one?
games.why: he left the chief of them standing, so they might turn to it. tomorrow, they do.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you do only because you've always done it. Hold it up the way Ibrahim looked at the row of images, and ask it plainly: why are you here, and what can you actually do? If you pray, ask for clear eyes.

wordCard.voice: Ibrahim. He broke his people's idols, left the biggest one standing, and let it wait for their questions.

orig.note: Arabic: "a big one of theirs" (21:58), the idol Ibrahim left standing.

carryVoice: Your line: ask the big one. Ibrahim left one idol standing so the question would stay in the room. Day thirty-three, done.

sources.q: What are these images unto which ye pay devotion?
